findings.claim: “Homing” is repeatedly attributed to “Fiona Benson” (33 mentions across L1, L6, L8).
findings.truth: “Homing” is by Liz Berry. Fiona Benson is a real poet but has no poem in this cluster.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) contents p.3 and p.17: 'Homing – Liz Berry'.

findings.claim: Brontë's Earth 'has watched over the speaker since childhood'.
findings.truth: The poem says only 'I've watched thee every hour'. There is no reference to childhood.
findings.evidence: Full text of 'Shall earth no more inspire thee' (allpoetry.com/Shall-Earth-No-More-Inspire-Thee).

findings.claim: Brontë quotation “thy sunny youth”, used in content, a mark scheme and two flashcards.
findings.truth: The phrase does not appear anywhere in the poem. Nearest real wording: 'I know my sunshine pleases'.
findings.evidence: Full 7-stanza text of the poem; AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.11 quotes no such phrase.

findings.claim: “Homing” is described as a poem about landscape: 'specific plants, weather patterns, and textures of land'.
findings.truth: The poem is addressed to a dead relative who was taught to hide her Black Country accent. Its extended metaphor is a locked box of speech; its imagery is dialect words, 'vowels ferrous as nails', 'consonants you could lick coal from'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.17.

findings.claim: “Name Journeys” attributed to Grace Nichols and read as names travelling 'from Africa through the Caribbean to Britain' under slavery.
findings.truth: “Name Journeys” is by Raman Mundair, born in India and raised in Manchester. It moves from Rama, Sita and Draupadi to her Punjabi landing on 'infertile English soil' and her name as 'a stumble / that filled English mouths'. Its form is a loosened ghazal, not free verse with onomatopoeia.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.14.

findings.claim: “Like an Heiress” attributed to 'Sumia Jaama, a British-Somali poet' exploring Somali culture.
findings.truth: “Like an Heiress” is by Grace Nichols. Sumia Jaama has no poem in this cluster. The poem is a free-verse sonnet from a cycle written after a return visit to Georgetown, Guyana: 'eye-catching jewels', then 'a lone / wave of rubbish' and 'like a tourist'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.22.

findings.claim: “A Wider View” read as an argument that dual heritage 'expands rather than fragments identity', with 'imagery that draws from both Sri Lankan and English landscapes'.
findings.truth: The poem is set in Leeds. Seneviratne imagines her great-great-grandfather there in 1869 — 'back-to-back' houses, 'cholera', 'twelve hours combing flax' — and the title comes from his craving 'the comfort of a wider view'. The last stanzas move to Leeds today via the 'Dark Arches'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.16.

findings.claim: “A Century Later” attributed to 'Arundhathi Subramaniam, an Indian poet based in Mumbai', and read as a poem about returning to a place changed by time.
findings.truth: “A Century Later” is by Imtiaz Dharker. Published 2014, it answers Wilfred Owen's 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' and responds to Malala Yousafzai: 'the school-bell is a call to battle'; she 'takes the bullet in the head' and 'walks on'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.18.

findings.claim: Berry's train poem read as a Black man 'surrounded by white passengers who refuse to acknowledge his presence' — 'proximity without connection'.
findings.truth: The poem is a friendly conversation. A Quaker woman 'startled me' by speaking first, talks of 'racial brotherhood', and is 'So sincere she was beautiful'. The racism is her unmeant assumption that Jamaica is in Africa, which he answers with the joke 'Ireland is near Lapland'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.13.

findings.claim: Robinson's paradise is 'tastes, sounds, warmth, rhythms … cooking a dish, playing a song, telling a story'.
findings.truth: The poem's images are 'white sands, green hills and fresh fish', and the imperatives 'trace', 'smell', 'hum'. Food, music and storytelling are not in it.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.21.

findings.claim: “The Jewellery Maker” attributed to Patience Agbabi and read as an extended metaphor for 'the craft of memory and storytelling', with technical vocabulary 'soldering, setting, polishing'.
findings.truth: The poem is by Louisa Adjoa Parker, a writer of English and Ghanaian heritage. It is a literal portrait: an inherited trade ('like his father before him'), 'sits straight-backed' like 'a surgeon', tools 'neat as soldiers', and a wife whose one piece of jewellery is 'plain' and 'worn thin'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.19.

findings.claim: “Thirteen” read as 'an elegy for a particular moment of youth' capturing 'the joy and the danger' of an estate.
findings.truth: The poem is about being stopped by police at thirteen and mistaken for a man. It is written in the second person: 'cornered', 'praying', 'fear condenses on your lips', and the assembly officer's 'supernovas' turn out to be 'dying stars'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.23.

findings.claim: Femi's estates described as 'North London estates' (content and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Femi grew up on the North Peckham estate, which is in Peckham, south London.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.23: 'grew up on London's North Peckham estate'.

findings.claim: The title of “With Birds You're Never Lonely” is 'something said to the speaker — perhaps by a parent or grandparent', whose 'voice persists … beyond death'.
findings.truth: The phrase comes from a young Maori woman the speaker meets in New Zealand, who learned it from her grandfather. No relative of the speaker and no death appear in the poem.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.20.

findings.claim: “Pot” attributed to Imtiaz Dharker and read as a metaphor for 'how society shapes individuals (especially women)'.
findings.truth: “pot” is by shamshad khan (AQA prints title and name in lower case). Commissioned for Manchester Museum, it addresses a Nigerian pot in the collection: cultural repatriation, colonial looting, 'you're not really one of us', the wish to 'shatter' the display glass, and a dedication linking the pot to prisoners held without charge (2007).
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.15.

findings.claim: 'He was exiled from England for his views.' (Shelley)
findings.truth: Shelley left for Italy in 1818 by choice and never returned. He was not banished.
findings.evidence: Standard biography.

findings.claim: Eliot quotation “dark as funeral trains”, used in content, a collapsible revision tip and two flashcards.
findings.truth: The phrase does not appear in 'In a London Drawingroom'. The 19-line poem's nearest images are 'All hurry on & look upon the ground' and 'The world seems one huge prison-house & court'.
findings.evidence: Full text (litcharts.com/poetry/george-eliot/in-a-london-drawingroom); AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.12 confirms 19 lines.

findings.claim: The form/structure/language toolkit repeats the wrong attributions throughout (Benson, Agbabi, Jaama, Dharker's pot, Nichols's 'Name Journeys').
findings.truth: All five names corrected to Liz Berry, Louisa Adjoa Parker, Grace Nichols, shamshad khan and Raman Mundair, with examples drawn from the real poems.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) contents p.3.

findings.claim: Recommended comparison pairing 'Nichols + Jaama', with a matching knowledge check and practice question.
findings.truth: Jaama is not in the cluster. The real pairing of those two poems is Mundair ('Name Journeys') + Nichols ('Like an Heiress').
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) contents p.3.

findings.claim: Wordsworth quoted as “Have I not reason to lament?”
findings.truth: The poem's closing sentence is 'Have I not reason to lament / What man has made of man?'. The truncation adds a question mark that is not in the text.
findings.evidence: Lyrical Ballads (1798) text of 'Lines Written in Early Spring'.

findings.claim: Flashcard asks 'What is the first step of Russell's four-step language method?'
findings.truth: There is no Russell. The four-step method is the lesson's own, unattributed.
findings.evidence: L6 content_html n26 carries the method with no attribution.

findings.claim: Flashcard asks about 'Berry's “From Lucy: Englan' Lady”'.
findings.truth: That is a different James Berry poem and is not in this cluster. The cluster poem is 'On an Afternoon Train from Purley to Victoria, 1955'.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) contents p.3.

findings.claim: Peterloo described as 'killing 15 and injuring hundreds' (glossary and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Long-standing sources say 15; research since 2005 puts the death toll at 18, with 400–700 injured. Both figures circulate in teaching resources and neither affects an English Literature mark.
findings.evidence: Michael Bush, 'The Casualties of Peterloo' (2005).

findings.claim: Practice questions are labelled '4 marks — Quote Analysis' and '8 marks — Extract Analysis'.
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B has one 30-mark comparison only; the unit's '30 marks — Anthology Comparison' label is correct. The 4- and 8-mark labels are internal scaffolding and 'Extract Analysis' is misleading, because the named poem is printed in full and no extract is used. Hand to the question-type relabel workstream rather than editing 24 items here.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Paper 2 'Questions', Section B.

findings.claim: KC[1]: 'What unusual technique does Brontë use by having the Earth speak directly to a human?' Keyed answer: 'Apostrophe'. Distractor: 'Dramatic monologue'.
findings.truth: Both are defensible and the AQA teacher guide names dramatic monologue: 'It can be seen as a dramatic monologue with the speaker being a personification of nature.' A student who has read AQA's own guide would pick the distractor and be marked wrong. Options: (a) reword the stem to name the direct address ('Which technique describes Earth addressing “thee” throughout the poem?'), or (b) change the keyed answer to dramatic monologue and replace that distractor. Recommend (a) — it is one field and preserves the glossary term 'apostrophe' used elsewhere in the lesson.
findings.evidence: AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.11.

findings.claim: Lesson 3 is titled 'Migration & Displacement' but its third poem, once correctly attributed, is Dharker's 'A Century Later' — a poem about girls' education and Malala, not migration.
findings.truth: The edits rewrite the lesson's connective prose to a defensible shared idea (holding on to yourself where you are not welcome), which is true of all three poems. The cleaner fix is a lesson-title change, which is a DB field outside this raw dump and Tom's call. Lesson 4's title 'Memory & Time' is a looser fit for Parker/Femi/Antrobus but survives.
findings.evidence: L3 title vs AQA/Collins 'Worlds and Lives Poetry Cluster Teacher Guide' (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-8702-WORLDS-AND-LIVES-POETRY-CLUSTER-TG.PDF) p.18.

findings.claim: Roughly 40% of the unit's prose changes under these edits, and every lesson has a narration manifest (22–30 blocks each).
findings.truth: The whole unit needs re-narrating after the edits land. Narration ids and block counts are unchanged by every edit, so re-narration is a straight re-run rather than a re-cut. Do not flip these lessons back to students until the audio matches.
findings.evidence: L1–L8 narration_manifest lengths 22/22/22/22/22/27/30/30.

summary: The unit teaches the correct 15 poems but names the wrong poet for five of them (Homing, Name Journeys, Like an Heiress, A Century Later, The Jewellery Maker, pot — six poems, two of the invented attributions naming poets with no work in this cluster), and the analysis written for each of those poems describes a poem that does not exist. Two quotations are fabricated (“thy sunny youth”, “dark as funeral trains”), one flashcard cites an invented critic (“Russell’s four-step method”) and one cites a James Berry poem outside the cluster. Every exam claim checked against AQA 8702 is correct: Paper 2 Section B, one named poem printed plus one of the student’s choice, 30 marks, and no false “AO2 is not assessed” claim anywhere. 280 edits fix all 22 FIX findings; three items need Tom’s judgement.
